title: 17 Million Letters. 855 Black Women. They Did It in Half the Time.

beats.text: In February 1945, in Birmingham, England, warehouses were filled with mail that no one had delivered. About seventeen million letters and packages, for American soldiers fighting in Europe.

overlays.hook: Seventeen million letters. *Nobody could deliver them.*

beats.text: Some had been sitting there for months. Soldiers were going without word from home, and the Army believed it was hurting morale.
The Army estimated the job would take six months. Then it sent eight hundred fifty-five Black women to do it.
They cleared it in three.
They were the six thousand eight hundred eighty-eighth Central Postal Directory Battalion. The Six Triple Eight.
When the war began, women could serve in the Army through an auxiliary corps. In July 1943, Congress made it the Women's Army Corps, the WAC.
Black women joined it too. But for most of the war, the Army kept them at home, and many were given menial jobs.

visual.caption: Black WAC officers and enlisted women, 1943

beats.text: Mary McLeod Bethune, the educator and adviser to the President, pushed to change that. So did First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt.
They wanted a role for Black women in the war overseas.
In 1944, the War Department agreed. It created a new unit, made up of Black women.
The women came from across the country. Most were African American, and some were of Caribbean and Mexican descent.

visual.caption: Black WAC officers and enlisted women, 1943

beats.text: They went through four to six weeks of basic training, and then weeks more of specialist training, before they were sent overseas.
To lead it, the Army chose Major Charity Adams.
She was from Columbia, South Carolina, and she had been in the first officer candidate class of the women's corps. She was now the highest ranking Black woman officer in the Army.
On February 3, 1945, the first of them sailed for Britain, on the liner Ile de France.
On February 12, they landed at Greenock, near Glasgow in Scotland, and went south by train to Birmingham.

visual.caption: U.S. Army nurses arriving at Greenock, Scotland, 1944

beats.text: Three days after they landed, two generals came to inspect them.

visual.caption: Maj. Charity Adams and Capt. Abbie Campbell inspect the first women to arrive, February 1945

beats.text: The battalion had eight hundred fifty-five women in five companies, both officers and enlisted.
There was a headquarters company and four more, A through D. And they ran their own camp from the start.
And they did not only sort mail. They had their own cooks, mechanics, medics and military police.
What they found in Birmingham was a mess.
The mail was stacked in cold, dark buildings, with the windows blacked out against air raids. There was little heat.
Rats had gotten into packages of food sent from home.
And so much of it could not be delivered. Letters were addressed only to a first name, or to a nickname, or to "Junior, U.S. Army."
There were about seven million Americans in Europe, and they kept moving. In one account, seven thousand five hundred of them were named Robert Smith.
So the women built a system. They kept index cards for soldiers, with their serial numbers and their units, and updated them as men moved.
In time, the card file grew to seven million cards.
Mail for a soldier who had been wounded, or moved, or killed, had to be traced through those cards, one name at a time.
They worked three shifts, eight hours each, seven days a week. Each shift handled about sixty-five thousand pieces of mail.
Their motto was simple. No mail, low morale.
Not everyone welcomed them.
One day, a white general came to inspect, and found only some of the women in formation. He asked where the rest were.
Adams told him. A third were on duty, a third were sleeping, after the night shift.
He said he was going to send a white first lieutenant down to show her how to run things.

visual.quote: I'm going to send a white first lieutenant down here to show you how to run things.

beats.text: Her answer became famous. Over my dead body, sir.
Her staff found an official memo warning commanders against language that stressed racial segregation. The general backed down.
When the Red Cross tried to put the women in a separate hotel in London, Adams refused that too.

visual.caption: Charity Adams with Black WAC trainees, 1943

beats.text: And when they were offered separate facilities, they ran their own. Their own dining hall, their own beauty shop, their own snack bar.
By May 1945, the backlog in Birmingham was gone. The Army had expected six months. It took them three.
The war in Europe had just ended. And there was more mail waiting in France.
In the spring of 1945, the battalion moved to Rouen.
There, they marched in a parade in honor of Joan of Arc, in the marketplace where she had been burned at the stake.
In Rouen, they were housed in old French barracks, and they worked in cold, damp buildings that were no better than the ones in England.
The people of Rouen watched American women in uniform, Black women, marching through their square.
In July, three of them, Mary Bankston, Mary Barlow and Dolores Browne, were killed in a jeep accident.
They are buried at the Normandy American Cemetery, among the very few women buried there.
The Rouen backlog was cleared too. In October 1945, the unit moved to Paris.
In February 1946, the last of them returned to the United States. The battalion was disbanded at Fort Dix, New Jersey.
There was no parade. No public ceremony. No welcome home.
Many of them went to college on the GI Bill and became teachers, nurses, and civil rights workers.
Charity Adams left the Army as a lieutenant colonel. In 1989, she published her memoir, One Woman's Army.
In 1981, some of the veterans went back to Birmingham, where the mayor honored them. In 1996, the Smithsonian's National Postal Museum honored Charity Adams.
In 2019, a blue plaque went up at King Edward's School in Birmingham, where the women had worked through the mail.
Slowly, the country began to remember. A monument at Fort Leavenworth in 2018. A unit commendation from the Army in 2019.
In 2021, the Senate passed a measure to honor them.
In February 2022, the House of Representatives voted four hundred twenty-two to zero to award the battalion the Congressional Gold Medal. President Biden signed the bill that March.
In 2023, the Army renamed Fort Lee, in Virginia, as Fort Gregg-Adams, in part for Charity Adams.

visual.caption: Lt. Col. Charity Adams, Fort Gregg-Adams

beats.text: On April 29, 2025, the medal was presented in Emancipation Hall at the U.S. Capitol. More than three hundred descendants of the women were there.

visual.caption: The Congressional Gold Medal ceremony, U.S. Capitol, 29 April 2025

beats.text: Charity Adams's son accepted it on her behalf.

visual.caption: The Congressional Gold Medal of the 6888th

beats.text: And in December 2024, a film about them, The Six Triple Eight, put their story in front of millions of people who had never heard it.
Seventeen million letters. Three months.

visual.caption: The Congressional Gold Medal of the 6888th

beats.text: They worked in the cold and the dark, against a deadline and against the doubts of their own Army.
And every letter they moved meant a soldier somewhere finally heard from home.
That was the Six Triple Eight. Subscribe for more.

notUsed: Number of women: 855 (Wikipedia, History Hit) vs "over 800" / "800 girls" (National WWII Museum, NARA caption): script uses 855.
The Greenock photo shows U.S. Army nurses in 1944, not the 6888th; it is captioned as such.
Exact date and cause of the Rouen accident: left at "July, jeep accident"; no detail.
Promotion of Adams to colonel in 2025: not confirmed.
